newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Peace brings nervous Guatemalan left into open.
newsitem.headline: Peace brings nervous Guatemalan left into open.

text.p: Mario, a 37-year-old student leader wearing a rebel bandana around his neck, pointed to the imposing National Palace where on Sunday Guatemala officially ended its 36-year guerrilla war.
"If you'd gathered like this before, you would have been dragged behind there and you wouldn't have got out," he said, rolling his eyes.
Thousands of Guatemalans marched to the main square Sunday hours before the government and Marxist rebels signed a historic treaty ending one of Latin America's longest-running and guerrilla wars.
The marchers sought to shake off memories of the nightmare years of the 1970s-1980s when army intelligence chiefs masterminded persecution of leftists from an office in the National Palace.

For the first time in their lives, they were openly chanting support for the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels, a 1,700-member force that unites four guerrilla groups, the first of which went underground in 1962.

URNG commanders returned to Guatemala City on Saturday for the first time in decades to take part in the peace signing ceremony with President Alvaro Arzu. They were met with jubilation by supporters at the airport.
Their troops will disband in the New Year, and many plan to become militants of the political party the URNG will forge.
The extent of civilian backing for the rebels has been a permanent mystery of the war, because open sympathy for the rebels was effectively silenced by military repression.

However, hundreds of grassroots organisations have slowly gathered strength over the past 15 years, including widows and relatives of slain activists, unions, peasants and land rights organisations, as well as Indian groups in a country where 60 percent of the population is Maya.
Pressure from such groups has been among the factors that pushed the peace process to a conclusion.

But Sunday's celebrations contained an undercurrent of scepticism about the peace accords, which promise cuts in the army and strengthened Indian rights but need billions of dollars and goodwill to fulfil.
As he talked, Mario kept an eye on riot police guarding the plaza and feared his photograph may have been taken by right-wing spies. He refused to give his last name.

He said a dossier containing information on his activities as a left-wing organiser was once held in the National Palace's notorious "archives," put together on suspected opponents of hardline military rule.
For most of its history, the palace was largely an adjunct of the military high command that ruled Guatemala with an iron fist for almost three decades until 1986.

On Sunday evening, leaders from Latin America and Spain and dignitaries from around the world gathered for a gala ceremony in the palace courtyard to sign a treaty that will bring an end to a conflict in which 140,000 people were killed.
Even as they bellowed support for the URNG, marchers -- including students, unionists, Indian peasants from the rural highlands, and urban squatter groups -- worried how long the euphoria would last.
"Let's see if they comply with what they sign, if peace is more than just a piece of paper. I doubt it," said Ermelinda Ramos, 35 who has secretly supported the URNG for 10 years.
There was even scepticism of the URNG leadership, some supporters of which worried they may be sold out by the rebels when the URNG becomes a peacetime political party.
The Marxist rebels have a vaguely defined political platform and few concrete military gains to show for years of low-intensity warfare against army and police targets.
They have also committed their own atrocities and, until they called a ceasefire in March, hampered business by blowing up vital oil lines and disrupting commercial trucking routes.
